topic: Override Keyword for Virtual Function Safety
explanation:
The `override` special identifier is a modern C++ feature used to explicitly declare that a member function in a derived class is intended to override a virtual function from a base class. It acts as a clear statement of intent to both human readers and the compiler, enhancing code clarity and robustness in class hierarchies.

Scott Meyers' key insight is that `override` is not just syntactic sugar but a critical safety mechanism. Its primary purpose is to prevent a common and insidious bug where a derived class function *fails* to override a base class function due to a subtle signature mismatch. Without `override`, this mistake results in a new, independent virtual function being created, leading to incorrect polymorphic behavior that is often only discovered at runtime.

The mechanics are straightforward: when the compiler encounters a function marked `override`, it performs a series of checks. It verifies that a base class contains a virtual function with the exact same name, parameter types, const-qualifier, and reference-qualifier. It also ensures the return types are covariant. If no such function exists in any direct or indirect base class, the compiler issues a compilation error, transforming a potential runtime logic error into an easy-to-fix compile-time diagnostic.

In practice, using `override` makes maintaining and refactoring class hierarchies significantly safer. For example, if you modify the signature of a virtual function in a base class, every derived class that used `override` for the old signature will immediately fail to compile. This instantly provides a to-do list of all locations that must be updated, preventing the old, now-unrelated derived functions from silently coexisting with the new base function. It is a fundamental tool for ensuring polymorphic correctness.

A common pitfall is simply neglecting to use it, reverting to C++98-style silent failures on signature mismatches. Another mistake is believing that `virtual` in the derived class function serves the same purpose; while `virtual` is necessary for the function to be part of the virtual dispatch chain, only `override` provides the compiler-enforced guarantee that you are actually overriding something.
practical_example: When refactoring a large system, a developer might change a base class method `virtual void process(const Data& d)` to `virtual void process(Data&& d)` to add move semantics. By using `override` in all derived classes, the compiler will immediately flag every subclass implementation, forcing developers to update their `process` methods and preventing subtle bugs where the old overload is called instead of the new one.
